title: The training principles series: good form
summary: NH defines good form as technique that targets the intended muscles, keeps you safe and pain-free, and is reproducible; performance is deliberately excluded. He separates objective form rules everyone must follow (no lumbar rounding on deadlifts, no flared elbows on bench, no knee valgus) from subjective, leverage-dependent choices (hip height, knee travel, stance, elbow tuck) to tune once advanced.

claims.claim: Form (technique) is the way you execute a movement; good form should target the muscles you want, keep you safe and pain-free, and be reproducible every rep.
Performance is not a criterion of good form; good form may make you lift less weight.
Dive-bombing squats or rounding the upper back on deadlifts can let some people lift more, but it is bad form.
For quads on the high-bar squat: the more vertical the torso and the more forward knee travel, the more quad involvement.
Form is partly subjective because of individual leverages, but that is no excuse for bad form.
Objectively bad form 100% of the time: rounding the lower back on deadlifts, flaring the elbows on bench press, knee valgus (knees caving) on squats.
Subjective, leverage-dependent form elements: deadlift hip height, degree of upper-back rounding, squat knee travel and hip angle, bench touch point and elbow tuck.
New lifters should first master the objective form rules; that alone greatly reduces injury rates.
Subjective form tuning matters once advanced, either for performance or targeting muscles; assess each set afterward (where did I feel it?) and adjust.

On the squat, a narrower stance with toes forward maximises forward knee travel and quad recruitment; toes out recruits more hamstrings and glutes, increases range of motion and puts more pressure on the hips.
Choose your form by weighing which risks you accept for the results you want.
Bodybuilding is experimentation: any technique that works and is safe (both required) belongs in your toolbox.
Whether pulling with a rounded back is safe has been debated enough; NH finds the subjective tweaks more interesting.
